name: Face shields and visors
summary: A clear visor on a headband or hard hat that covers the face against splashes, sparks and debris; for impact and chemical work it goes over safety glasses or goggles, never instead.
uses: Grinding and cut-off wheels: worn over safety glasses, to keep flying particles off the face (OSHA 3151; OSHA shipyard eTool)
Pouring acid, solvents or pool chemicals: over indirect-vent goggles (CCOHS eye protectors)
Breaking CRTs and glass, or opening anything that may burst or spray: over goggles (OSHA 3151)
Blood and body-fluid splash: OSHA 1910.1030 accepts a chin-length shield with a mask; CDC rates indirect-vent goggles best and a shield the wider-cover alternative (CDC eye protection)
On its own it doesn't give adequate impact protection; it guards against splash and spray, and with goggles or glasses it adds impact and splash cover (OSHA 3151)
Electrical arc flash: OSHA 1910.269 requires protective equipment with an arc rating at or above the arc's heat energy, so use only a shield marked arc-rated (OSHA 1910.269)
identify: A curved clear or tinted visor, usually polycarbonate, on ratchet headgear or on brackets that clip to a hard hat; it should run from above the eyes to below the chin and wrap round the sides (CCOHS eye protectors; OSHA 3151). US: shields that meet Z87.1 are marked Z87 or Z87+ (NIOSH eyewear bulletin). Canada, CSA Z94.3 class 6: 6A impact and splash, 6B radiation filter, 6C high heat, 6D electric arc (HexArmor CSA; CCOHS eye protectors). Europe, EN 166 (EN ISO 16321 takes over from November 2025): 3 for splash, 8 for short-circuit electric arc, 9 for molten metal and hot solids (uvex EN 166). Tinted shields for torch work need a shade number (OSHA 1910.133). Arc-flash shields for electrical work carry an arc rating; OSHA's power-line rule asks for at least 8 cal/cm² in some cases (OSHA 1910.269). Look-alikes: thin disposable visors from pandemic stock and craft or cosmetic shields have no impact rating unless marked; uvex warns that disposable visors without EN 166 marking don't give enough UV protection (uvex FAQ).
test: Look through the visor against the light and replace it if scratched, pitted, broken or bent (CCOHS eye protectors; NC State eye PPE). Check that the headgear or hard-hat brackets hold the visor firmly where you set it. Replace damaged parts only with identical parts from the original maker (CCOHS eye protectors). Fit: it should reach below the chin and above the eyes and wrap the sides of the face (CCOHS eye protectors); for splash work CDC says it should cover the crown and chin and wrap to the ears (CDC eye protection). Put safety glasses or goggles on first, then the shield (OSHA shipyard eTool; UW-Madison eyewear). Clean with mild soap and water and air-dry, unless the maker says otherwise (NC State eye PPE). Some shields aren't impact-rated at all (NC State eye PPE): with no Z87, Z94.3 or EN 166 mark, treat it as a splash guard only.

decay.note: Estimate: no maker's shelf life was found. Visors scratch with use and must then be replaced (CCOHS eye protectors); headgear ratchets and hard-hat brackets can wear and crack. Boxed spare visors should keep longest if dry and dark.

improvise: Protect the eyes first: safety glasses or goggles do the essential job, and a shield only adds to them (OSHA 3151; UW-Madison eyewear). A full-face respirator covers eyes, nose and mouth against splash (CCOHS eye protectors). OSHA says face shields and welding helmets go only over primary eye protection (OSHA shipyard eTool). An auto-darkening welding helmet has a grind mode meant for grinding, with safety glasses or goggles worn under it (Lincoln Viking manual). A sheet of clear plastic propped between you and the job might turn a light splash aside, but nobody has tested it for splash or impact, so keep your safety glasses or goggles on. Home-made visors cut from bottles or clear folders may deflect a splash but have no impact rating: never wear them instead of glasses. Against electrical arc flash an unrated shield is not protection: OSHA's rules call for arc-rated face shields (OSHA 1910.269), and the real answer is to make the circuit dead first.
